prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength are interrogated without a trap-induced shift

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration I stated in round 1: B040, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Nothing in the second-round material weakens the scientific case, and the exchange has sharpened how I would defend it. The invention is a specific physical idea, trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength where the lattice light does not shift the clock transition. That removed the trade-off between the signal-to-noise of many atoms and the freedom from motional and trap shifts that had been the privilege of single ions. It has been realised in more than one species, and independent laboratories now compare these clocks at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, so the result does not depend on interpretation or on a single group. Seven of eight files reach this configuration from different opening choices, and I do not treat that count as evidence in itself. What persuades me is that the same reasons recur from an atomic physicist, an experimentalist in another field, a theorist and the chair, and that the strongest objections have specific answers. In one sentence for the citation: the comb (2005) is the ruler that reads optical frequencies, the 2012 prize rewarded control and measurement of individual quantum systems, and this prize rewards a way to interrogate a large neutral-atom ensemble at optical frequency without a systematic shift from the trap. I would word the citation around the invention and its development and not around a record figure, since other groups keep improving the numbers.
statement.case_against: The distinctness objection is still the real one and I would not wave it away: Ye shared in the comb lineage through his association with Hall, and a reader could see a third precision-spectroscopy award. I think it fails on the physics, but it is a judgement, and the citation has to carry the argument. The pair also leaves out Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the supplied material does not settle the relative weight of Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy work, so I cannot claim a finer division than complementary roles. Part of the motivation, the redefinition of the second, has not happened, so the citation must not lean on it. Finally, I am a theorist in superconducting circuits and not an atomic-clock specialist, so on priority questions among lattice-clock groups I rely on Lindroth and Kroll.

responses.point: Danielsson alone prefers B018 for the IceCube diffuse flux, says B040's distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes needs more argument and that its consequences are partly prospective, and lists B040 first among his alternatives.
responses.response: I take B018 seriously: a new messenger channel and an unpredicted signal are what the discovery criterion is about, and your two-name credit is compact. On the distinctness argument you asked for, I would say the clock does not refine the comb or ion control, because the new element is the magic-wavelength condition for a large neutral ensemble, which neither earlier prize addressed. On prospectiveness, the 1e-18 agreement and comparisons are already realised; only the redefinition of the second awaits a decision by bodies outside this committee. My difficulty with B018 now is the one you list yourself, that the dominant sources are unidentified and AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND are not covered, so the citation would have to be confined to the diffuse flux. That could be defended, and I would not oppose it on merit, but I think B040 is the more settled result this year. Since you would not object strongly to B040, I ask you to consider whether the remaining gap between us is one of timing and not of merit.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B040 but records that the 2005 and 2012 prizes may make it a third step in one measurement lineage, and discloses a research stay in Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I do not think your stay with Hall requires recusal on B040. Hall is not among the credited names, and you document no tie to Katori or Ye; the committee should record the disclosure, as you have done. I would also resist reading the lineage argument as decisive. The lineage runs through frequency measurement and control of single particles, while the lattice clock departs from it at the step that matters, the choice of a trapping wavelength at which the transition is unperturbed. If a continuation reading is correct, it should also be possible to say what the earlier prizes already contained, and I cannot find the magic-wavelength condition in either. I would ask you to accept the species-neutral wording below, because it states exactly that.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce proposes a species-neutral citation naming the lattice clock concept, and asks me to say why strong coupling in circuits is a distinct discovery.
responses.response: I agree with species-neutral wording. Strontium, ytterbium and others realise the concept, and naming one would start a priority argument the evidence does not need. On your question about circuit QED: scientifically it is distinct from macroscopic quantum tunnelling, since it concerns strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single photon, dispersive readout and the architecture built on them. But I am conflicted on B055 through WACQT, and I will not argue for it beyond this one sentence. I also think the boundary with the 2025 prize and the missing Girvin and Devoret-side credit make it a harder case than B040 this year, so I do not ask the committee to weigh it against the clock.

responses.point: Lindroth would divide the citation by roles, asks whether independent 1e-18 comparisons suffice for maturity, and says the relative weight of Katori and Ye is not settled by the supplied text.
responses.response: On maturity I side with the comparisons you describe: several laboratories, with independent clocks agreeing at that level, are the demonstration, and the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision downstream of it. On roles, I would keep them out of the citation text. Katori made the conceptual step and the first strontium lattice clocks; Ye took the platform to the accuracy frontier. Writing a division into the citation would require a precision the supplied evidence does not give, and Mehlig's point about avoiding record figures argues the same way. The committee's record can state the roles, with Lemonde, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups acknowledged, while the citation stays on invention and development.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B040 and keeps B061 and B022 as fallbacks, and says the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 2016 prize weigh on B061.
responses.response: We agree on the attribution problem and I stay with it. I still think B061 is scientifically distinct from the 2016 prize, since time-reversal-invariant topological insulators with protected edge states are a different class with their own experimental confirmation, but three names cannot honour the HgTe proposal and the Z2 work together, with Zhang deceased and Bernevig and Hughes outside. If the committee wanted a second part in this round I would not support B061 in its current three-name form, so I leave it as a fallback and not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether Danielsson can join a B040 award; I count only what his file says.
Whether the priority question among Katori, Ye and other lattice-clock groups can be settled with the supplied material, given the Katori and Ye split that Lindroth and Olsson raise.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing; I treat it as downstream of a demonstrated result.
Whether a second part is warranted at all; I see no candidate with a clean three-name credit and no overlap that I would support alongside B040.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT at Chalmers, which is close to the circuit QED work in B055 (Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize), so I recuse myself from deliberation and any vote on B055 and on related superconducting-circuit material. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, or the topological insulator candidates (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp). Olsson noted I am a Chalmers colleague; that is an institutional link and does not bear on B040 or B018.
